rules.statement: A library that does no ASP.NET Core work must not take a `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` framework reference or reference `Microsoft.AspNetCore.*` packages; it should depend only on `Microsoft.NETCore.App` plus the specific `Microsoft.Extensions.*` packages it needs.
rules.why: A framework reference bought only for constants or helpers forces every console app or worker that uses the library to install the ASP.NET Core runtime.
rules.check: Look for a `<FrameworkReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.App" />` or `Microsoft.AspNetCore.*` usings or package references in a project whose code handles no HTTP server types.

rules.statement: Append query parameters to an endpoint URL by percent-encoding each value with `Uri.EscapeDataString` and joining with `?`, or with `&` when the URL already has a query.
rules.why: This follows RFC 3986 without an ASP.NET Core query helper, and it keeps any query the endpoint already has.
rules.check: Look for query strings built by string concatenation without `Uri.EscapeDataString`, or code that always uses `?` even when the URL may already contain a query.

rules.statement: Accept an authority or endpoint URL only when it is `https`, or `http` on a loopback host (`Uri.IsLoopback`), and validate the raw string as well as the parsed `Uri`: the string starts with its scheme, contains no whitespace and has no fragment, and an authority also has no query.
rules.why: Plain `http` is allowed only to the same machine, for tests against an in-process provider. Checking the raw string catches input that `Uri` parsing would quietly normalize.
rules.check: Look for endpoint or authority validation that checks only the parsed `Uri`, allows `http` to hosts that aren't loopback, or doesn't reject fragments, whitespace, or a query on an authority.

rules.statement: When consuming OIDC discovery, require the returned `issuer` to equal the configured authority by ordinal comparison, require `token_endpoint` and `jwks_uri`, and validate every endpoint member that is present against the endpoint rule. Report any violation as a protocol exception.
rules.why: OIDC Discovery §4.3 requires the issuer to match exactly, and an unchecked endpoint member could point the client at an insecure or unintended host.
rules.check: Look for a case-insensitive or normalized issuer comparison, required metadata members that go unchecked, or endpoint members used without scheme or host validation.

rules.statement: Take protocol-client credentials from a named, keyed secret-key provider (a key ring) that the caller identifies on each call, not from bound configuration values.
rules.why: Credentials in configuration put secrets in configuration and leave no way to rotate them. Key rings rotate and can be held in a key management service.
rules.check: Look for client secrets or signing keys read from `IConfiguration` or options, instead of being resolved from a keyed `ISecretKeyCollectionProvider` named by the caller.

rules.statement: Use named `int` constants for HTTP status codes instead of casting `HttpStatusCode` members to `int`, and keep a status code as `int` when the public type exposing it is `int`.
rules.why: Named constants read better than enum casts, and typing the value as `HttpStatusCode` would only cast straight back to the public `int`.
rules.check: Look for `(int)HttpStatusCode.X` expressions, or internal status-code properties typed as `HttpStatusCode` that are then cast to `int`.

rules.statement: A cache of remote metadata or key sets must collapse concurrent misses into one fetch. On a failed refresh it serves the last good value only within a bounded stale lifetime and backs off for a minimum interval; it rate-limits forced refreshes (such as an unknown `kid`) by that same interval; and it never relaxes validation in order to serve a stale value.
rules.why: This bounds the load on the provider and the exposure to stale data, and it keeps a stale value from ever bypassing validation.
rules.check: Look for caches that fetch once per concurrent caller, serve stale values with no age limit, allow forced refreshes without a rate limit, or skip validation on the stale path.

rules.statement: When importing a provider's JWKS for signature verification, skip each unusable key (not an object, not a parseable JWK, `use` other than `sig`, `key_ops` without `verify`, a non-asymmetric or unknown key type, or material that fails to import). Refuse the whole set if it carries private or symmetric material, has two usable keys with the same `kid`, or has no usable key at all.
rules.why: RFC 7517 §5 lets a client ignore keys it can't use. A set exposing private or symmetric material, or with ambiguous `kid`s, can't be trusted.
rules.check: Look for JWKS import code that throws on a single unusable key, accepts private or symmetric keys, allows duplicate `kid`s, or accepts an empty usable set.

rules.statement: Model client authentication methods as an open strategy collection: register each strategy with `TryAddEnumerable`, select it by its method name, and throw at construction when two strategies share a name.
rules.why: Vocabularies are open, so a new method is a new registration with no library change, and duplicate names must fail fast.
rules.check: Look for a closed `switch` or `enum` over authentication methods, registrations made with `AddSingleton` instead of `TryAddEnumerable`, or selection that silently picks one of two duplicate names.

rules.statement: A `private_key_jwt` client assertion (RFC 7523) must have `iss` and `sub` equal to the client id, `aud` set to the provider's issuer as a single string (not the token endpoint URL), a `jti` of 16 random bytes in base64url, `iat` and `nbf` at now, and `exp` 60 seconds later.
rules.why: RFC 7523bis and FAPI 2.0 require the audience to be the issuer, and a short fixed lifetime with a random `jti` limits replay.
rules.check: Look for an `aud` set to the token endpoint or to an array, a missing or low-entropy `jti`, or a configurable or long assertion lifetime.

rules.statement: Sign client assertions only with asymmetric keys, never with a MAC or `none`. Filter the client's algorithm preference list to what the provider advertises in `token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported`, and refuse to start when a configured algorithm entry is blank, is `none` or repeats.
rules.why: A MAC or `none` must never sign an assertion, and bad configuration should fail at startup instead of at request time.
rules.check: Look for symmetric keys allowed as assertion signing candidates, `none` accepted, or no startup validation of the configured algorithm list.

rules.statement: In a protocol client, return an OAuth error response (a JSON object with a string `error`, at any status) as a value. Throw a protocol exception, wrapping the cause as the inner exception, for transport, timeout, size, JSON or malformed-response failures. Let caller cancellation propagate as `OperationCanceledException`, and throw `InvalidOperationException` for configuration errors.
rules.why: Callers need errors such as `invalid_grant` as values, while real failures and misconfiguration should be exceptions they can tell apart.
rules.check: Look for code that throws on OAuth error responses, wraps caller cancellation in another exception, drops the inner exception, or uses a protocol exception for a configuration error.

rules.statement: An outbound HTTP client to an identity provider must not follow redirects or use cookies (`AllowAutoRedirect = false`, `UseCookies = false` on its primary handler), and it must cap the size of every response body.
rules.why: Otherwise a hostile or misconfigured provider could redirect the client or exhaust its memory.
rules.check: Look for an `HttpClient` or handler registration that leaves auto-redirect or cookies on, or response reads with no size cap.

rules.statement: Parse a protocol response as JSON only when its body is non-empty and its media type is a JSON type (`application/json` or `application/jwk-set+json`), and treat an empty body as having no JSON whatever its media type.
rules.why: A successful response may legitimately be empty (for example revocation under RFC 7009 §2.2), and a body with the wrong media type shouldn't be parsed as JSON.
rules.check: Look for JSON deserialization of response bodies with no media-type check, or code that fails on an empty success body.

rules.statement: An authorization-code token request must carry a PKCE `code_verifier`.
rules.why: The decision requires PKCE for every authorization-code grant.
rules.check: Look for an authorization-code request type or builder where `code_verifier` is optional or missing.

rules.statement: Model token requests as an abstract base type carrying the shared parameters (`scope`, the repeated RFC 8707 `resource`), with one sealed subclass per grant, so a new grant is added by subclassing instead of by changing a closed type.
rules.why: Vocabularies are open, so a new grant type must be addable without changing library code.
rules.check: Look for a single token request type with a grant enum or switch, or grant request classes that aren't sealed.

rules.statement: Don't add `ConfigureAwait(false)` to awaits in library code whose callers are server-side hosts without a `SynchronizationContext`.
rules.why: The no-`ConfigureAwait(false)` rule holds because these callers have no synchronization context.
rules.check: Look for `.ConfigureAwait(false)` added to awaits in server-side library code.

rules.statement: Read text files with an overload that takes an explicit strict encoding, such as `File.ReadAllText(path, SecureEncoding.UTF8)`, never with the overload that takes no encoding.
rules.why: The banned-API analyzer forbids the overloads that take no encoding.
rules.check: Look for `File.ReadAllText(path)` or similar calls that pass no encoding.
